title: Clinical Management of Intracameral Silicone Oil: A Comprehensive Guide
summary: Intracameral silicone oil is a challenging complication following vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade. Proper management requires careful assessment of intraocular pressure, corneal health, and the urgency of removal.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Intracameral silicone oil (ISO) refers to the migration of silicone oil droplets from the posterior segment into the anterior chamber, typically through a patent or surgically created peripheral iridotomy/iridectomy, or secondary to pupillary block. It is most commonly associated with heavy silicone oil or high-viscosity oil tamponades. Prevalence ranges from 2% to 20% post-vitrectomy, depending on the indication (PVR, giant retinal tears).

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Secondary open-angle glaucoma (oil emulsification in the trabecular meshwork)

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Observation if small, asymptomatic, and stable IOP.
Step 2: Medical management (topical hypotensives) if IOP elevated.
Step 3: Surgical washout via limbal paracentesis using irrigation/aspiration.
Step 4: Mechanical removal using bent 27G needle or cannula.
Step 5: Peripheral iridotomy management if blockage is suspected.

content.explanation: Observe if stable, Irrigated if corneal touch, Lower pressure (glaucoma meds), Surgical removal if refractory.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Silicone oil in the AC can cause silent corneal endothelial cell loss (endotheliopathy).
Perform specular microscopy if possible to assess endothelial count before major interventions.
When removing oil via paracentesis, consider using a viscoelastic (OVD) to protect the endothelium during aspiration.
Always check the posterior segment; ensure the retina is attached, as oil in the AC may be a sign of posterior migration issues or failure of tamponade.
